text:
MADISON – As Wisconsin's electricity costs continue to outpace those of most of its Midwestern counterparts and voters point to the cost of living as their biggest worry, candidates vying to be the state's next governor are highlighting the issue in policy proposals and campaign ads.

The focus on utility rates in the Badger State also comes after Democrats in Virginia and New Jersey won governor races last fall on a platform that included a promise to address utility costs.

The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel asked the candidates – seven Democrats competing in the Aug. 11 primary and one Republican who will face the winner in the Nov. 3 general election – about their utility policy priorities, how they would seek to balance consumer costs against the need for a reliable energy grid and what they would look for in appointees to the state's Public Service Commission.

In Wisconsin, the three-member PSC regulates the state's utilities, including approving rate increases or decreases and major construction projects. Commissioners, appointed by the governor and approved by the state Senate, serve staggered three-year terms.

In the case of candidates who have received more than $1,000 in campaign contributions from utility-aligned interests, the Journal Sentinel asked what voters should discern from that financial support.

Here's what they had to say.

Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes (Democrat)

Barnes has made his pledge to freeze utility rates if elected a central component of his policy platform.

The former lieutenant governor has also said he would place limits on utilities' lobbying activity and executive pay, shift the costs of shuttered coal plants away from ratepayers and offer state tax credits for energy efficiency home improvements.

In his "Freeze the Rates" plan announced in March, Barnes said he would only appoint commissioners to the PSC who would freeze utility rates, denying any proposed increases from utilities. Utilities experts have said the promise may be legally questionable and unworkable.

He pledged to sign into law a ban on utility companies using ratepayer dollars for lobbying and political expenses, along with a pay cap for utility company executives.

"Utility companies have rigged the system to boost their profits and pay for the massive salaries of wealthy executives while Wisconsinites have had to cut back on essentials like food and prescriptions to keep the heat on," Barnes said in a statement, pledging to "take on monopolies like We Energies who are exploiting ratepayers to line their own pockets."

Barnes also said he would require utilities to cover the debts of shuttered coal plants, ensuring they are not passed to ratepayers. His plan also calls for removing barriers to renewable energy projects, state investments in battery storage, tax credits for energy efficiency home improvements and the elimination of reconnection fees for low-income families.

Former DOA Secretary Joel Brennan (Democrat)

Brennan, who led the Department of Administration in Gov. Tony Evers' first term, listed three priorities in this area.

First, he said, he would reinstate what is known as integrated resource planning to guide utilities in meeting energy demand while considering environmental impact, cost-effectiveness and grid reliability.

Brennan said he would also tie what utilities are allowed to earn to affordability metrics and implement a payment scheme for data centers, requiring them to pay 100% of their own energy costs, generate 30% of their own power and commit 30% of their demand to utility response programs.

"Those three things alone would fundamentally change how energy costs get managed in this state," Brennan said.

The PSC "exists to balance what utilities need to stay financially healthy with what families can actually afford," Brennan said, adding the balance is currently broken. Brennan pledged to appoint commissioners "who take both sides of that equation seriously."

Brennan also said he'd support legislation to require utilities to reach 100% clean energy by 2050, with all infrastructure built with Wisconsin union labor.

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (Democrat)

The county executive's top priority is "making energy more affordable for Wisconsin families while ensuring the grid remains reliable and prepared for future growth," a spokesman said.

Crowley said he'd do that by lowering costs through energy efficiency, expanding weatherization programs, making clean energy technologies more accessible and ensuring large energy users, like data centers, cover their extra costs rather than passing them to residential ratepayers.

In appointing PSC commissioners, Crowley's campaign said he would look for "individuals with strong technical expertise, a commitment to transparency, and a demonstrated understanding of consumer protection, long-term energy planning, and the importance of creating and sustaining good-paying union jobs.

"David believes the Public Service Commission should be focused on affordability, reliability, innovation, accountability, and workforce development, not simply maintaining the status quo," the spokesman said.

An analysis of campaign finance records shows Crowley has received $500 from the WEC Energy Group PAC and $100 from the Alliant Energy PAC – both during his 2018 Assembly reelection bid.

State Rep. Francesca Hong (Democrat)

Hong's campaign did not respond to questions from the Journal Sentinel, but the state representative has discussed energy policy in public forums and on her website.

In a recent forum hosted by groups including 350 Wisconsin, Hong said the PSC must be more reflective of the public interest, in part by consulting with public health experts, legal experts and environmentalists on the challenges faced by those most affected by rate increases.

Hong also said she would bar any ratepayer dollars from being used for lobbying or executive pay raises.

As a member of the state Legislature, Hong has introduced bills she also intends to pursue if elected governor. Those include a bill that would cap utility costs at 2% of an "energy-burdened" household's income and create a relief fund to subsidize those costs.

Hong is the lone candidate in the field who supports a one-year moratorium on data center construction in Wisconsin. As governor, she would require any new data center construction to be done with union labor. She would require projects to generate "long-term community benefit" and to fund new renewable or clean energy infrastructure that is publicly owned.

Hong also supports allowing local governments to run their own public utilities

Former WEDC Secretary Missy Hughes (Democrat)

Hughes, who led the Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. for most of Evers' tenure as governor, pledged to implement "a comprehensive energy vision for Wisconsin's future that prioritizes affordability, modernization, reliable delivery, and renewable power."

"Our first priority must be to make sure that we lower utility costs for families, communities and small businesses," Hughes said.

The former Organic Valley executive placed blame on President Donald Trump and the Republican-led Congress where U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany serves for "new tariffs, higher gas prices and increased costs" and stalled progress on clean energy production.

Hughes said she'd seek three primary qualifications in PSC appointees: "technical and substantive policy expertise; independence from political ideology and special interests; and an understanding that energy is a necessity and high costs burden Wisconsin workers, families and businesses."

She also pledged to elevate the commission's Office of Energy Innovation to serve as a planning hub.

Hughes said she would continue to work toward Evers' goal of reaching 100% carbon-free electricity by 2050 by adding more wind, solar and hydroelectric energy to the state's portfolio.

Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez (Democrat)

Like Barnes, Rodriguez has proposed some form of a rate freeze, but hers would be done temporarily, through an executive order, to give ratepayers "breathing room" while implementing a longer-term plan.

"She will make sure corporations pay their own energy costs instead of sticking Wisconsin residents with the bill and invest in cheaper, cleaner energy sources that actually bring monthly bills down over time," her campaign said. "She will also give homeowners and small business owners the ability to sell energy back to the grid and put people in charge of overseeing utilities who look out for residents instead of utility company profits."

Rodriguez said she would look for PSC commissioners "who wake up every morning thinking about how to lower costs for Wisconsinites," with a "track record of standing up for consumers, and the willingness to say no to rate increases that make families subsidize corporate energy use."

The state can maintain a reliable grid with lower energy bills as long as large corporations and data centers pay their share of costs, Rodriguez's campaign said, adding that her campaign would invest in "cheaper, cleaner energy" paid for by the corporations that benefit from the upgrades, including data centers.

An analysis of campaign finance records shows Rodriguez has received $13,800 from the WEC Energy Group PAC. Rodriguez received $500 as an Assembly candidate in 2020.

She then received $12,800 in October 2022, after officially joining the ticket with Evers for that year's midterm election after winning the August lieutenant governor primary (Barnes did not seek reelection that year, opting instead to run for U.S. Senate).

Under Wisconsin law, a party's candidates for governor and lieutenant governor may pool their campaign accounts after the primary and effectively run as one operation. At that point, WEC Energy Group had already maxed out to Evers' 2022 campaign fund.

Rodriguez received another $500 from the PAC as lieutenant governor in 2023.

Asked about the contributions, a campaign spokeswoman said the lieutenant governor "has always made decisions about legislation or policy based on what’s best for Wisconsin, not a campaign contribution."

"What tells you where she stands is what she is actually proposing to do," the spokeswoman said. "Those are the policies of someone who is looking out for Wisconsinites. In contrast, Congressman Tom Tiffany has taken tens of thousands of dollars from utility interests over his career in Congress and has done nothing to lower costs for Wisconsin families."

State Sen. Kelda Roys (Democrat)

"Combating climate change is our century's challenge, and Wisconsin has every advantage we need to lead," Roys said in a release announcing her energy platform. "Wind and solar are now the cheapest and fastest new sources of energy – meaning the transition to clean power isn't just good for our environment, it's the smart financial choice for Wisconsin families and our economy.”

Roys said she would appoint commissioners to the PSC "who are consumer watchdogs, not utility company lapdogs," increase the commission's staff and boost funding for the Citizens Utility Board, which advocates on behalf of ratepayers.

The state senator pledged to continue efforts to power the state with 100% clean energy by 2050, expand the state's energy-saving Focus on Energy effort, invest in the "clean tech" business sector and enact a host of regulations on data center development.

Roys backs expanding on data center regulation introduced by Democrats last year that included renewable energy usage requirements, sustainable building standards, a pay rate for project construction workers and the creation of a new energy category, rate and tariff for data centers.

An analysis of campaign finance records show Roys received $500 from the Alliant Energy PAC in 2010 when she served in the Assembly.

U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany (Republican)

Tiffany has taken aim at energy costs since he entered the race, including a digital ad buy in February blasting the PSC's actions during Evers' administration.

The Republican candidate for governor placed blame in part on Evers' "carbon-free by 2050" plan for more than $2 billion in PSC-approved rate increases.

"Yet even as rates continue to rise, Wisconsin’s in-state power generation has not materially increased," Tiffany said. "Families are paying more and getting nothing in return. I will change this approach and ensure Wisconsin prioritizes reliable baseload power generation and affordable energy."

As governor, Tiffany pledged to stop the closure of "reliable, baseload power plants."

"I will protect our farmland from being taken over by massive solar, wind, and data center projects, and I will appoint commissioners to the PSC who are accountable to Wisconsin ratepayers. Wisconsin will also lead on new nuclear technology to lower costs," he said.

Tiffany said he'd look for commissioners who "committed to protecting Wisconsin farmland, putting ratepayers ahead of rubber-stamping utility rate hikes, prioritizing reliable baseload power over dependence on foreign technology from China, and restoring accountability and transparency to the PSC."

An analysis of state and federal campaign finance records shows Tiffany has received about $11,500 from the WEC Energy PAC, $2,000 from the Alliant Energy PAC and $3,000 from the Xcel Energy PAC from his time in the state Legislature and in Congress.

"The Democrats’ PSC approved more than 70% of requested utility rate hikes, and Mandela Barnes and Sara Rodriguez served under Governor Evers through it [all] without saying a word. text:
CRANBERRY TWP — Electric vehicles are common sites on the township’s busy roads, and Pennsylvania leads the nation in the number of EV charging stations, but most are along the interstate system and the turnpike.

The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation is now offering $25 million in National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure “Community Charging” funds to help businesses, organizations and developers build public EV charging stations in Western Pennsylvania communities. The NEVI program will cover 80% of the cost of a charging station project and applicants will have to cover the remaining 20%.

PennDOT Secretary Mike Carroll was joined by Southwestern Pennsylvania Commission executive director Rich Fitzgerald and officials from the township and county in announcing the available funding.

Carroll said the state received $173 million National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure, or NEVI, funding, and $70 has been spent on charging stations along interstate highways and the turnpike. Of the $100 million available for community EV charging projects statewide, $25 million has been allocated for Western Pennsylvania and the rest is available in other regions. EVs and plug-in hybrids can use the charging stations.

Aug. 21 is the deadline to submit proposals, and award announcements will be made in October or November. Information about the program and application process can be found at pa.gov/evcommunity.

“Organizations who visit this website can connect with operators and builders to partner on their projects and deliver alternative fueling options for residents,” Carroll said.

He said PennDOT worked with the Southwestern Pennsylvania Commission to conduct a survey to identify priority locations in Western Pennsylvania, and worked with other regional planning organizations for surveys in other regions.

“Hundreds of thousands of EVs are in the possession of our residents across the state, and so many of those folks don’t have the ability to charge their vehicles at home,” Carroll said. “These charging stations that exist now on our interstate network and interstate look-alikes will be complemented by charging stations in communities.”

PennDOT and the state are national leaders in putting NEVI money to good use, and no state money is involved in the program, he said.

The elimination of federal tax credits for EV purchases has reduced sales, but EV sales are not going to stop, he added.

“To think of a great community like Cranberry, I couldn’t think of a more vibrant place in which they really would have a lot of opportunities in this community to have the NEVI charging stations,” Fitzgerald said.

Existing EV charging stations are required to be no more than a mile from interstate exits and have fast charging speeds. The community stations can have different speeds, said Colton Brown, of PennDOT.

Township manager Dan Santoro said he believes parties from the township will be interested in pursuing NEVI funding. He said 25,000 people work in the township, and Interstate 79, the turnpike and Route 19 bring a lot of people to the township.

Leslie Osche, chairwoman of the Butler County Commissioners, said the NEVI funding is a great opportunity for businesses and beneficial for the many people who drive EVs. The charging stations also would benefit EV drivers visiting the county.

text:
Clean energy fought the law, and clean energy won.

Despite constant pressure on multiple fronts from the Trump administration- including but not limited to pushing false “clean coal” rhetoric, undercutting tax credits, and literally paying companies to walk away from offshore wind leases- carbon-free power sources not only continue to come online, but comprise more and more of our electrical system.

The United States drew more power from solar panels than from coal generation plants in May, the first time that’s ever happened. Solar accounted for 12.8% of all U.S. electricity last month, while coal contributed a near-all-time low of 12.2%. Solar and battery energy storage represented 91% of new capacity added to the U.S. grid in the first quarter of 2026, including 7.8 gigawatts (GW) of new photovoltaic capacity, despite back-and-forth federal policies and an uncertain regulatory climate. In a particularly interesting wrinkle, states won by President Trump accounted for 74% of all solar capacity installed in Q1 2026; Texas, Florida, Ohio, Indiana, Michigan, Arizona, and Mississippi all rank among the top 10 states for new solar additions. The U.S. now boasts more than six million solar farms nationwide.

The pace of deployment will slow as federal incentives phase out, but the market is sending a strong signal now: Cost and speed-to-power matter more than anything else. Not everyone cares about “clean and green,” but when one type of technology is less expensive and can get a project online faster than another, that’s where money will flow, tax credits be damned. Look no further than Cypress Creek’s $3.5 billion financing of a complex, three-stage Arkansas project, with a “big tech” offtaker lined up for its first two phases. Investors have the stomach to plunk billions into clean tech to enable deep-pocketed developers, and there’s no sign they won’t continue to do so.

“In a world of fluctuating fuel prices, energy buyers have made it clear that they want the security, low cost, and speed of solar and storage,” concurred Darren Van’t Hof, interim president and CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA). “Yet, as power demand skyrockets, political and regulatory attacks are slowing down the exact resources we rely on. Impeding the only sector that is actively building new power is a reckless gamble that will only drive electricity bills higher. The stakes are simply too high for Washington’s permitting gridlock to continue.”

Trump campaigned on promises to address electricity demand growth by cutting regulatory red tape and speeding up permitting, but hasn’t delivered, instead throwing up myriad roadblocks. What will it take to convince the administration that solar and storage are the future… And the future has arrived?

Welcome to the Factor This Brief, a weekly collection of energy industry finance and development updates, delivered straight to your inbox on Monday mornings and hosted in a not-so-brief fashion here on Factor This, featuring the people, projects, and technology driving our electric future.

Thanks for checking it out. If you like what you see or want to recommend a story for next week, drop me a line. In the meantime, may your next bowl of cereal stay crunchy for way longer than you expected.

PJM Adds Largest Standalone Storage Site

PJM Interconnection, the largest grid operator in the United States and a frequent punching bag for everyone who has an opinion about how the people who work there can do their jobs better, is adding the largest-ever standalone energy storage asset to its system.

Last Thursday, Elevate Infrastructure and investor ArcLight Capital Partners celebrated the ribbon-cutting of the now-operational Prospect Power Storage, a 150 Megawatt (MW) / 600 Megawatt-hour (MWh) battery energy storage system (BESS) in Rockingham County, Virginia.

“Today marks an important milestone for Elevate and for Virginia’s energy future,” observed Joshua Rogol, CEO of Elevate. “Prospect Power demonstrates how Elevate executes utility-scale battery storage at scale to strengthen grid reliability, support economic growth, and help meet the increasing energy needs driven by data centers, artificial intelligence, and electrification.”

“Battery storage is playing a growing role in supporting a reliable, resilient, and diverse grid,” added Stu Bresler, COO of PJM. “This project increases battery storage capacity within PJM by more than 50%, marking a significant milestone for energy storage in our region. Resources like this add flexibility to the grid and help support reliability as demand continues to grow.”

Prospect Power is fully contracted under a 15-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with local utility Dominion Energy Virginia. Beyond its contributions to grid reliability, the BESS is expected to deliver lasting benefits to Rockingham County through revenue-sharing payments and property tax contributions.

ArcLight and Elevate acquired Prospect Power in January 2026. Its completion marks the latest milestone in Elevate’s expanding platform. In March, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities selected the company’s 150 MW / 600 MWh Garden State Reliability Project as part of the Garden State Energy Storage Program. In April, Elevate closed a $50 million Energy Transition Supplier Finance Facility supporting a solar and battery storage project contracted to power a data center, and the company also submitted 7,600 MWh of new battery energy storage into the latest PJM queue process.

Distributed Solar and Storage Pipeline Attracts $300M Investment

Nexamp, the largest fully-integrated distributed generation and community solar provider in the U.S., has closed on a $300 million aggregation securitization facility with Crédit Agricole CIB that will support the deployment of distributed solar and energy storage projects in its pipeline. The construction-to-term facility offers Nexamp a scalable, flexible source of project-level funding suited to the volume and pace of its DG deployment aspirations.

“This facility underscores the strength of Nexamp’s long-standing business model and the growing recognition of distributed solar and storage as a mature, attractive asset class,” noted Zaid Ashai, CEO of Nexamp. “By pairing competitive construction financing with flexible takeout options, we can move faster to deliver the power that communities and businesses need—while opening the door for a wider range of institutional investors to support the energy transition.”

According to Nexamp, the aggregation securitization facility will be used to finance a diversified portfolio of community solar, commercial and industrial (C&I), and other distributed generation and storage assets across multiple regions. These projects will provide locally sited, flexible capacity that supports grid reliability, helps mitigate congestion, and expands access to energy savings for households, businesses, and public sector customers.

Now with More Geysers?

Calpine, a business unit of Constellation, has announced the completion of a 25 MW expansion project at The Geysers geothermal complex in Sonoma County, California. The addition follows the completion of a 38 MW energy storage system at the site in 2024. The new capacity will generate enough electricity to power over 25,000 homes each year.

“As California’s electricity demand continues to grow, investments in reliable, around-the-clock renewable energy are more important than ever,” assessed Aimee Blaine, senior vice president of Calpine’s geothermal region. “The Geysers is one of the nation’s most important geothermal resources, and this expansion reflects our commitment to strengthening grid reliability while advancing California’s clean energy goals.”

The Geysers is the world’s largest operating geothermal complex, generating electricity by tapping natural steam reservoirs deep beneath the earth’s surface. For more than 65 years, the site has provided clean, geothermal energy across California. Of the 25 MW expansion, 18 MW will be directed to Clean Power Alliance (CPA), which serves customers across Southern California, providing reliable, around-the-clock renewable power as demand for clean electricity continues to grow. The remaining 7 MW, which were brought online last year, are being supplied to MCE to support Bay Area residents and businesses.

“Clean Power Alliance is committed to delivering dependable clean energy to our customers, and geothermal power plays an important role in providing around-the-clock renewable electricity,” said Matthew Langer, chief operating officer at Clean Power Alliance.

The recent expansion was completed under a Project Labor Agreement (PLA) with local labor unions, ensuring the work was performed by a highly skilled craft workforce under strong labor standards.

Community Solar Portfolio Lands Tax Equity Financing

Distributed independent power producer (IPP) GS Power Partners has closed on more than $51 million in tax equity financing from funds managed by AB CarVal to support an approximately 41 MWdc portfolio of eight community solar projects in New York, Maryland, and Illinois.

The transaction is part of a broader tax equity partnership between Greenprint Capital and AB CarVal, through which Greenprint structured and executed the financing. In addition to expanding access to affordable clean energy, the projects are expected to generate long-term economic benefits for the communities that host them.

“Distributed generation tax equity portfolio transactions are financial milestones that reflect the sophistication and creativity we bring to bear,” said Nick Kamphaus, General Counsel of GS Power Partners. “Closing this complex financing across three states underscores our strength in connecting capital to productive energy projects, and our commitment to delivering DG solar assets that meet the highest standards of compliance and accountability.”

CRC-IB acted as financial advisor to GS Power Partners. Stoel Rives LLP served as legal counsel to GS Power Partners, and Leverage Law Group acted as legal counsel to Greenprint Capital.

Big Battery Comes Online in Arizona

EDP Renewables North America and Salt River Project (SRP), a not-for-profit public power utility serving more than 2 million people in central Arizona, are celebrating the completion of Flatland Energy Storage, a 200 MW / 800 MWh BESS in Coolidge, Arizona.

Located in Pinal County, Flatland Energy Storage will enhance grid flexibility and improve energy reliability in the region. Flatland Energy Storage is the largest BESS within the EDP Group, with the capacity to power approximately 44,500 Arizona homes.

“Energy storage plays a critical role in maintaining a reliable and resilient electric grid, especially as demand continues to grow,” said Sandhya Ganapathy, CEO of EDP Renewables North America. “Projects like Flatland Energy Storage ensure power is available when it’s needed most, while also delivering meaningful, long-term benefits to the communities that host them.”

“Flatland Energy Storage is part of SRP’s all-of-the-above approach to providing reliable, affordable, and sustainable power to our customers,” added Bobby Olsen, SRP associate GM and chief power system executive. “SRP will continue to invest in battery energy storage resources as part of its growing resource portfolio.”

Flatland Energy Storage represents more than $20 million in local and regional economic impact over its lifetime, including $19.2 million in revenue to support local public services and infrastructure, more than $1.3 million in regional spending, and approximately 142 jobs during construction.

text:
Globally, electricity generation emits 37 GtCO2 yr−1, with 1.5 Gt coming from the USA1,2. Power plants also release air pollutants including primary fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and key precursors of secondary PM2.5: nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs)3. Natural gas supplies the largest share of total US electricity at 43%, whereas coal supplies 16% (ref. 4). Annual premature mortality estimates from fossil electricity generation range from 4,000 to 9,000 people in the USA, most of which come from coal-fired power plants5,6. Postcombustion carbon capture and storage (CCS) can remove upwards of 90% of the CO2 from the exhaust (that is, flue gas) at pulverized coal and natural gas combined cycle (NGCC) power plants after the fuel is burned7,8. CCS systems that separate CO2 from the flue gas after the fuel is burned have been used in refineries and in the chemical industry but have not been adopted at a large scale among US power plants7. Little is known about the maximum potential of CCS across existing US thermoelectric power plants or the potential air pollution and resulting human health effects associated with such retrofits, yet these are key considerations for determining how and where to prioritize CCS development and deployment.

CCS is challenging at power plants for several reasons including trace impurities in the flue gas (for example, SO2 and NO2) which degrade solvents, the comparatively low concentration of CO2 and low-pressure environments requiring a large absorber column for CO2 capture resulting in an energy penalty for solvent regeneration7. Historically, the most extensively studied solvent for postcombustion CCS in the literature is monoethanolamine (MEA)9, which absorbs CO2, thus separating it from the remainder of the flue gas10. MEA is a first-generation solvent, whereas CESAR1, a mixture of 2-amino-2-methyl-1-propanol11 and piperazine12, is a second-generation solvent that has higher stability and lower degradation13. At power plants without adequate emissions controls, SO2 in the flue gas will lead to unacceptably high solvent losses in amine-based postcombustion CCS systems, regardless of whether MEA or a second-generation solvent such as CESAR1 is used14. This means that, for some CCS retrofits to minimize solvent losses, additional emissions controls are necessary. Before postcombustion CCS, flue gas desulfurization (FGD) can be used to remove SO2, ideally to less than 1 part per million by volume (ppmv) levels7,14,15. Thus, power plants that pursue a CCS retrofit may also install new emissions controls (for example, enhanced water wash systems) to minimize solvent degradation and emissions. The net impact of these emissions controls may yield substantial air pollution and human health cobenefits. However, these benefits may be counterbalanced by the tendency of amine-based solvents to undergo oxidative degradation in CCS systems, releasing ammonia (NH3) and other volatile compounds16. SO2 and NH3 are precursors for secondary PM2.5, which contributes to air pollution-related premature mortality in humans17. To weigh the greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation value of postcombustion CCS in the USA and corresponding health cobenefits resulting from SO2 emission reductions against the health burdens due to NH3 emission increases, this study models a set of scenarios for postcombustion CCS at coal and NGCC power plants.

We compare the external costs and benefits of large-scale postcombustion CCS adoption in the USA through 2050, focusing specifically on the external costs/benefits of changes in human health burdens and climate forcing. We consider the effects of retrofitting both coal and NGCC plants with CCS to understand how they differ in terms of net external costs/benefits and total potential scale. Because solvents continue to evolve and improve, we compare results for both a first- and second-generation solvent, MEA and CESAR1, respectively. Our analysis accounts for heterogeneity in the mix of power plant types and in their air pollution impacts, as regional grids vary significantly within the USA. This study focuses on postcombustion CCS and does not include other alternatives such as precombustion capture and oxy-fuel combustion. Although various emission control technologies, such as acid wash and thermal reclaiming, can reduce NH3 emissions from amine-based CCS, the costs of these measures are substantial and uncertain18. Our analysis quantifies the health benefits of emission reduction, providing the basis for a cost–benefit analysis of control requirements and informing engineering decisions about solvent selection and control technologies.

This analysis brings together four main components, as shown in Fig. 1: (1) power plant CCS retrofit scenarios for coal and NGCC plants, (2) grid mix and generation scenario modelling, (3) plant-level emissions changes and (4) the quantification and monetization of human health and GHG emissions impacts. We convert the quantity of CO2 emissions avoided and net changes in air pollutant emissions to total external costs and health cobenefits or coburdens from CCS using the monetary value of carbon and the value of a statistical life, respectively19,20,21,22. A range of US dollar values per metric ton of CO2-equivalent are explored to reflect uncertainty regarding how or if these social costs will be considered in future decision-making. Economic and technological uncertainty regarding which plants are attractive candidates for CCS retrofits are captured by applying a range of constraints related to age and plant size. This approach enables us to compare the external benefits and burdens of CCS and determine the magnitude of CO2 emissions reductions that are possible if CCS is deployed across US power plants.

Nationwide power plant emissions

There are 479 coal-fired generators and these facilities produce 59% more CO2 emissions than the currently operating 1,971 NGCC generators23 (Fig. 2). However, anticipated coal plant closures are expected to alter this balance, absent any policy interventions that might delay such closures. Using National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) standard scenarios, we find that by 2030, NGCC plants are expected to produce 44% more CO2 emissions than coal plants24. The suitability of existing plants for CCS retrofit in 2025 varies by fuel type. We find that 73% of CO2 emissions from coal plants occur at facilities that do not meet even the least stringent criteria for economically viable CCS retrofits, as enumerated in Methods (<30 years old in the year 2025 and >100 MW), meaning that these plants may not be attractive candidates for CCS retrofits. In comparison, only 3% of NGCC CO2 emissions come from plants that do not meet the least stringent CCS criteria. This difference between NGCC and coal plants is primarily due to the age of the plants considered. The current average age of coal plants in the USA is 45 years old while the average age of NGCC plants is 22 years (refs. 25,26). This changes by 2040, as most of the NGCC and coal plants that do not currently meet the age criteria are anticipated to be retired. Assuming power plants retire at the ages specified in Methods, a greater share of coal generation is met by plants that meet CCS criteria over time in this model. In 2050, all NGCC and coal plants expected to be operating are suitable for CCS retrofit now, if the least stringent criteria for power plant age relative to 2025 are used.

The criteria used to select power plants for economically viable CCS retrofit have a direct effect on the quantity of CO2 emissions that can be captured and sequestered. In the present day, only 2% of total coal emissions and 21% of total NGCC emissions come from plants that meet the most stringent CCS criteria. The current fractions of CO2 emissions from NGCC and coal plants that meet criteria for CCS retrofit are shown in Table 1.

Location-specific emissions reductions and health impacts

Figure 3 shows the plant-level climate and human health effects of CCS retrofits on all applicable power plants in the present day using the minimum criteria (<30 years old and >100 MW). When comparing the climate benefits of CCS retrofit (Fig. 3a) to the human health effects using an MEA solvent (Fig. 3b), the CO2 reductions are more evenly distributed across many plants whereas a minority of plants, particularly coal, dominate the net human health benefits. This is because coal plants require FGD for emissions control before their flue gas has sufficiently low SO2 concentrations to be suitable for CCS. In the present day, we find that most power plants suitable for CCS are NGCC plants that already have relatively low emissions of SO2. Although these plants may be obvious economic targets for CCS, since they do not require additional emissions controls, the air pollution benefits of CCS retrofits are minimal whereas added emissions of NH3 contribute to human health burdens. The MEA NH3 emission factors used in the present study reflect an upper-bound case based on an earlier solvent system. It is possible to control NH3 emissions to low levels using an acid wash or a solvent with a higher stability27. Under the low ammonia emission scenario (Fig. 3c), which is the case for CESAR1 solvent use (Methods section ‘Power plant emissions’) or adding additional ammonia controls before emission to the atmosphere, CCS is likely to cause no substantial change to human health for most plants, alongside yielding substantial net benefits for several coal plants that are high SO2 emitters. The goal of CCS is to reduce GHG emissions, yet these results show that the effect of CCS processes on air pollutant emissions can have either human health cobenefits or coburdens. Next, the key is to understand potential trade-offs, which can be explored by monetizing health and climate impacts.

Comparison of monetized external benefits and burdens

Figure 4 shows the results of our external cost–benefit analysis, comparing the monetized external benefits and burdens from CO2 emissions reductions and changes in human health impacts if CCS is scaled up using an MEA solvent. Because MEA is a first-generation solvent, the results can be interpreted as a worst-case scenario for air pollution impacts. Results represent a mid-case renewable energy cost scenario in which all plants that meet the minimum criteria are retrofitted with CCS24,28. Results for additional renewable energy scenarios are in Supplementary Fig. 4. Using an MEA solvent, and assuming no additional NH3 controls are installed, the combined detrimental health effects of increased NH3 emissions from retrofitting coal and NGCC plants across the USA with CCS outweigh the benefits of decreased SO2 emissions at coal plants, leading to a net increase in overall air pollution-related human health impacts. However, the combined monetized CO2 emissions reduction benefits and human health impacts at the plant-level are nearly all positive when using a monetary value of carbon of US$190 tCO2e−1 (Fig. 4b). Under the MEA scenario, the only individual plants for which a CCS retrofit results in net external costs, in which monetized burdens outweigh the benefits, are the ones with the largest human health impacts in the northeastern USA. This is due to these plants being located near large population centres in the northeast, which causes comparatively large human health burdens when retrofitted with CCS that outweigh the monetized CO2 reduction benefits. There is substantial heterogeneity in these results based on the supplying fuel source (natural gas or coal), which is further explored in Fig. 5.

The balance of costs and benefits for CCS retrofits, not surprisingly, depends on the social cost assigned to CO2 emissions. We compare three different monetary values of carbon (US$190, US$51 and US$6 per tonne) which represent three weights that the US federal government has previously placed on CO2 emissions over the past decade19,20,21. When the monetary value of carbon is valued at US$190 or US$51 per tonne, the external societal benefits of CCS outweigh the costs. At US$6 per tonne, the external costs of CCS retrofits using MEA solvent outweigh the benefits for all study years. Given the health benefits of CESAR1 noted in Fig. 3c, the cumulative benefits outweigh any external costs. The results presented in Fig. 4 assume a constant monetary value of carbon across time. However, the weight placed on the monetary value of carbon should increase over time as a result of increasing marginal damages and global gross domestic product29. To represent the increasing monetary value of carbon over time, Supplementary Fig. 3 shows these results using a monetary value of carbon that increases from US$190 to US$310 per tonne between 2020 and 205021.

Sensitivity analysis of human health impacts

Figure 5 shows the range of human health effects from CCS retrofits on NGCC and coal plants with either an MEA or CESAR1 solvent. Most of the human health effects from coal-fired power plants come from plants that do not meet the least stringent CCS criteria of less than 30 years old and greater than 100 MW capacity (Fig. 5a). In the present day, CCS retrofits on applicable coal plants with an MEA solvent can decrease premature mortality associated with air pollutant emissions from these plants by 25% to 33% whereas CCS can increase premature mortality from NGCC plants by at least 12% and up to four times current levels (Fig. 5b). Up to a 67% decrease in human health impacts from coal plants could be achieved with a CCS retrofit using the CESAR1 solvent. The human health changes shown in this figure are due to decreased SO2 emissions and the range of possible increased NH3 emissions from degradation of the MEA and CESAR1 solvents in the CCS process. It is important to note, however, that these results do not imply that NGCC plants are more harmful to human health than coal plants. Rather, NGCC plants already have low SO2 emissions and do not require extensive flue gas pretreatment compared with coal, which limits the additional air-quality benefits that CCS retrofits can provide for NGCC. Consequently, even small increases in NH3 emissions from solvent degradation may result in proportionally larger health burdens for NGCC plants, whereas coal plants experience more substantial SO2 reductions that help offset the added NH3-related impacts. These results highlight the tension between minimizing private and external costs. Although NGCC plants are prime economic candidates for CCS since they require less pretreatment for air pollutants than do coal plants, increased NH3 emissions can increase the community-level health burdens from these plants. As shown in Fig. 3c, if a more stable solvent is used, or if NH3 is controlled before emission into the atmosphere, CCS may result in little change in premature mortality for most plants over current levels and substantial human health benefits for several coal plants that have high existing SO2 emissions. Detrimental health burdens and solvent degradation could be limited by further reducing NOx emissions to near-zero (<1 ppmv) levels, similar to SO2. The effects of reducing NOx to negligible levels from CCS plants are shown in Supplementary Fig. 10. Additional sensitivity analyses are shown in Supplementary Figs. 1–13 and Supplementary Tables 2–4.

In this study, we show that postcombustion CCS retrofits have the potential to substantially reduce total CO2 emissions from the US electric power sector, particularly from NGCC plants, but that the air pollution impacts may be more mixed in the absence of a transition to second-generation solvents. With the most basic size and age requirements for determining eligible plants, 97% of CO2 emissions are potentially addressable by adding CCS to NGCC plants compared with only 27% for coal plants. Under a mid-case renewable energy cost scenario, coal-fired power plants are projected to emit 79% less CO2 by 2050 relative to the present day, driven by retirement of coal plants and other shifts in the broader grid mix, whereas total nationwide CO2 emissions from NGCC plants are only expected to decrease by 7%. If NGCC plants continue to provide a large share of energy in the US electricity grid mix, targeting NGCC plants for CCS retrofits would probably be an effective way to address remaining fossil CO2 emissions in the power sector in addition to renewable power adoption. If all applicable plants for the minimum CCS criteria are retrofitted, 530 Mt of CO2 emissions could be mitigated annually based on present-day emission rates, cutting annual emissions from the US power sector by over one third.

The monetary value placed on CO2 emissions has fluctuated. Over the past decade, the US federal government has used monetary values of carbon ranging from US$1 to US$190 per tonne of CO2 (refs. 19,20,21). In this study, the monetary value of carbon and discount rates used in our cost-analysis directly affect whether the external societal benefits of CCS outweigh the costs. With a monetary value of carbon of US$190 and US$51 per tonne, the external societal benefits of CCS outweigh the costs regardless of solvent choice, but not at US$6 per tonne. Using a monetary value of carbon that differs from the academic literature in the price assigned to damages from CO2 emissions can underestimate the societal payoff of CCS.

There are uncertainties that arise in projecting results several decades into the future through 2050. Although we consider power plant retirement in our model, the decisions made by local governments, utilities and private companies to decommission power plants involve considerations beyond age, such as size, operational conditions, cost, demand, regulatory compliance and public perception30,31. Furthermore, where new fossil power plants will be built, particularly NGCC, and how they will be operated are both uncertain32,33. We focused exclusively on CCS retrofits at existing facilities for the purposes of this study. Our grid model assumes that plant-level emission factors will stay relatively constant, but emission factors can vary over time as a plant ages34. Within each region, we also assume that the share of individual power plants as a fraction of total generation for their specific fuel type does not change, which may not hold true in the future34,35,36.

A critical limitation of this analysis and any study of CCS health impacts at present is the scarcity of comprehensive emissions data from operating postcombustion CCS systems. Existing measurements are often from pilot-scale facilities, limited in duration, missing key variables for a scale-up analysis or conducted under conditions that may not be representative of full-scale commercial deployment at US coal and NGCC plants. We derived CESAR1 emission factors on the basis of limited operational data from a residue fluid catalytic cracking (RFCC) refinery37. We assume that these emission factors accurately reflect those in an NGCC or coal plant, however, more operational data are needed and should include several key elements. The MEA emission factors used in the present study are sourced from a 2010 study38 and are intended to represent upper-bound NH3 emissions consistent with earlier solvent systems. More recent studies of advanced solvents and process configurations indicate substantially lower NH3 emissions13,39,40. Future measurements should be conducted under representative flue gas compositions and operational conditions for NGCC and coal plants, as flue gas characteristics affect solvent performance and degradation. Studies should include comprehensive pollutant measurements both pre- and post-CCS for CO2, NO, NO2, NOx, PM2.5, SO2, NH3 and total VOCs along with relevant degradation products. Several replicate measurements across varying operational conditions are needed to characterize the full range of emissions, including steady-state operation, startup and shutdown phases and seasonal variations. Along with the pollutant measurements, corresponding flue gas flow rates and power generation data are needed for normalization. Continuous measurements over an extended period (weeks to months) are essential for capturing operational variability and solvent aging. As such additional empirical data become available, scale-up impact assessments like ours should be updated to improve understanding of the cost, air pollution and GHG trade-offs.

Although NH3 has emerged as a driver of potential air pollution impacts for some CCS systems, this problem is addressable, with recent literature showing that NH3 emissions can be reduced to low levels (<10 ppb) using an acid wash27. Future studies should explore the feasibility, costs and emissions reductions of additional NH3 control on CCS plants, such as acid washes or NH3 slip catalysts. As shown in Fig. 3c, reducing NH3 emissions through a stable solvent or added control could reduce human health burdens of CCS and potentially result in net health benefits for some plants. Our analysis focuses on MEA and CESAR1 as representative first- and second-generation solvents, respectively. Continued development of advanced solvents with even lower degradation rates and NH3 emissions could further reduce the health impacts quantified here. However, the fundamental trade-off between climate benefits from CO2 capture and health damages from degradation products will persist for any amine-based system, making solvent selection and emission controls critical considerations for CCS deployment. This study shows that postcombustion CCS using amine-based solvents can have human health cobenefits or coburdens depending on the solvent choice, fuel type, existing flue gas concentration and presence of NH3 emission controls. Ultimately, careful consideration of solvent choice and emission controls will be essential to maximize the climate and health benefits of CCS deployment.

Power plants suitable for CCS retrofit

The first step in quantifying the impact of large-scale CCS adoption is to determine which power plants are suitable for retrofit in the current year (2025), as some plants will be too old or too small for CCS to be practical. This allows us to quantify the long-term impact of potential near-term CCS retrofits. Power plant-level data came from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) eGrid41 and Power Plants and Neighboring Communities tool42, in addition to form 860 from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA)23. Together, these identified power plants with coal and NGCC generators and provided for each plant the latitude and longitude, age, capacity, capacity factor (CF), annual total generation and GHG and air pollutant emission factors per MWh generated. For a plant to be retrofitted with CCS, it must have a large capacity and CF to make the upfront investment worthwhile and must have a sufficiently long remaining lifetime to recoup the investment43. The International Energy Agency provided a set of scenarios for increasingly strict criteria based on age and capacity for applicable coal-fired CCS plants44. We use these criteria for coal and NGCC plants in the present study and add additional CF requirements. The CF requirements are necessary because NGCC plants can operate as either baseload or marginal generators depending on their geographic region and age45. The minimum CCS criteria used in this study are as follows:

(1)

<30 years and >100 MW (least stringent)

(2)

<20 years and >300 MW

(3)

<10 years and >300 MW

(4)

<10 years and >300 MW and >40% CF (most stringent)

Electricity grid model

In this study, we used an average electricity generation model to determine the quantity and location of power plant emissions in the continental USA. We used projections from the NLR standard scenarios24 to quantify electricity demand by region from now through 2050. NLR Cambium tool28,46 provides hourly demand and regional grid mixes through 2050. The spatial resolution for our grid model is the generation and emission assessment region-scale, used by Cambium. There are 20 regions in total which represent the electricity grid regions in the continental USA and have historically been a proxy for eGrid regions, although the region boundaries shifted in the Cambium 2023 release28. The temporal resolution for our grid model is hourly and projected from present day to 2050. Combining plant-level data from the EPA41,42 and EIA23 with regional load and grid mix data from NLR28,46, we determined the percentage of electricity that each individual plant provides for a given region and fuel type (that is, coal and NGCC). Applying our grid model, we assume that each plant supplies the same share of electricity for the given region and fuel type over time. We assign load to individual power plants based on their share in generation of that fuel type in that region. We consider that power plants will retire over time and assume that power plants retire at 52 years for coal and 40 years for NGCC based on the average retirement age of these power plant types30. If there are no plants of a given type in a specific region as a result of power plant retirement, we assign unmet load to applicable generators in neighbouring regions. We run two additional energy transition pathway scenarios through 2050 from NLR standard scenarios24, low renewable energy cost and high renewable energy cost, located in Supplementary Figs. 7 and 8. Additional information on the electricity generation model used in this study can be found in Supplementary Information section ‘Electricity generation model’.

Power plant emissions

Once electricity load was assigned to individual power plants, we quantified the GHG (CO2, CH4 and N2O) and air pollutant (NOx, SO2, PM2.5 and NH3) emissions for CCS and non-CCS plants. Emissions from non-CCS plants were calculated by multiplying the load assigned to each plant by the plant-level emission factors from the EPA42. Before emissions were calculated for CCS plants, we applied an increase in electricity load of 11% for NGCC plants and 16% for coal plants for CCS processes; the higher parasitic load for coal is due to its comparatively higher CO2 emissions per MWh of power generated and thus increased solvent requirements47. Parasitic load increases due to CCS processes were applied to the explicit calculation of primary PM2.5, NOx, CH4 and N2O emissions from plant-level emissions factors, leading to a slight increase in overall emissions38. We assume that the thermal and electrical energy requirements of the CCS system (11% energy penalty for NGCC plants and 16% for coal plants) are met by increasing the specific plant load for the retrofitted facility. However, alternative energy supply configurations are common in practice and could alter health impacts including installing auxiliary natural gas-fired package boilers to provide heat and/or electricity for the CCS system, drawing additional electricity from other plants in the grid system, or colocation with new, cleaner generation capacity that serves CCS energy requirements.

The solvent used in the CCS process can undergo oxidative degradation and the products of this degradation are expected to be emitted to the atmosphere in the absence of suitable emission controls. Although there are still gaps in knowledge about what compounds the solvent degrades to, amine-based solvents are primarily expected to produce NH3. There is considerable uncertainty in NH3 emission factors, with the literature reporting a wide range of possible values38,48,49,50,51. We consider two solvent choices in this analysis: a first-generation solvent (MEA) and a second-generation solvent (CESAR1). In an effort to consider the uncertainty in NH3 emission factors for amine-based solvents, we applied factors from ref. 38 for CCS plants using an MEA solvent, which reported the range of possible values as listed in Supplementary Table 1. We validated these with NH3 emission factors from IEAGHG50, which are lower but on the same order of magnitude (82 mg kWh−1 for coal plants). These are conservative estimates that can be updated in future studies if new NH3 controls are added, although this would result in potentially substantial additional private costs52,53. We derive NH3 emission factors for CESAR1 based on limited operational data of a RFCC refinery. Although we assume that these emission factors are applicable to NGCC and coal plants, more real-world operational data should be collected on NH3 emissions from power plants with CCS using the CESAR1 solvent. We find the CESAR1 emission factor for NH3 to be approximately 0.1 mg kWh−1, more than an order of magnitude lower than MEA. More information on these emission factors, including statistics on the operational data and emission factors, can be found in Supplementary Information section on ‘CESAR1 emission factors’, Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13 and Supplementary Tables 1–3. We assume that plants retrofitted with CCS are able to remove SO2 to near-zero levels to prevent unacceptably high solvent losses, thus making these emissions negligible for CCS plants7,14,15. We assume that CO2 removal rate is 95% for CCS plants, with lower and higher values of 90% and 99% used for sensitivity analysis54.

External costs and benefits of CCS

This study focuses specifically on external costs associated with GHG emissions and human health damages resulting from air pollution. To calculate the net change in GHG emissions resulting from large-scale deployment of CCS, we quantify the benefits of CO2 reductions assuming between 90% and 99% removal. We additionally consider that CCS may cause increases in other GHG emissions. We consider this for both direct power plant emissions, due to parasitic load, as well as upstream methane (CH4) leaks from natural gas use. For upstream CH4 leaks, we assume a leakage rate of 1% of gas produced55,56. For simplicity, we assume that this leakage rate is constant across the country. However, we recognize that this is an ongoing area of research and the true leakage rate varies between <1% and ~10%, depending on the region56. For each power plant, the resulting net change in 100-year global warming potential is quantified using AR6 values to adjust to CO2e emissions57. We used several monetary values of carbon to quantify the net climate benefits of CCS retrofit. There has been much debate about the appropriate monetary value of carbon to use in cost–benefit analyses. From 2017 to 2021, the US federal government used values ranging from US$1 to US$7 per tonne, then increased it in 2021 to an interim value of US$51 per tonne19,20. In 2024, EPA increased the monetary value of carbon to a present-day value of US$190 per tonne, increasing further to US$310 per tonne by 205021. We align our approach of quantifying monetized health and climate effects under different monetary values of carbon with ref. 58 and compare each of these values in our cost–benefit analysis to determine the climate benefits of CCS with various weights placed on the value of CO2. In this study, we assume that the monetary value of carbon refers to the monetary damages of a 1 tonne emission change in CO2 (ref. 21). However, we recognize that this term can also refer to monetary values for claiming incentives, demand for enhanced oil recovery or as an input to other processes. All calculations are done in 2024 US dollars. We assume a 2% discount rate for external social costs19 (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6 give additional discount rates).

The net changes in human health burdens—and resulting monetized damages—are driven primarily by premature mortality caused by primary and secondary PM2.5. We quantify the effects of CCS on human health using a reduced-order air-quality model, the InMAP Source–Receptor Matrix (ISRM)3,59,60. The ISRM transforms emissions of primary PM2.5 and precursors of secondary PM2.5 into total changes in PM2.5 concentrations at the grid cell-scale, with cell sizes varying between 1 × 1 km2 and 48 × 48 km2 (ref. 59). PM2.5 contributes to premature mortality, which is estimated using a correlation between PM2.5 concentration changes and all-cause mortality rates59. We run the ISRM using the base case emissions for all power plants in the USA through 2050, assuming no CCS, and again assuming all applicable plants are retrofitted with CCS. We consider that the US population will increase through 2050, applying a factor from the US Census for increased population by year61. We assume that the population increases uniformly throughout the country, as there are not population projections at a fine-enough resolution (1 ×1 km2) to consider regional variation in population changes or migration for input into the ISRM. We determine the human health effects by multiplying the change in premature mortality predicted by the ISRM with the value of a statistical life, which we assume to be US$13.8 million after adjusting for inflation22.

Whether CCS retrofit of an existing power plant results in net human health benefits or burdens depends on the type of power plant, local meteorology and proximity to population centres; there can be a decrease in premature mortality due to SO2 reductions or an increase driven by elevated NH3 emissions17. There can be further increases in human health effects due to increases in other air pollutants (for example, primary PM2.5 and NOx) from parasitic load causing an energy penalty. We ran the ISRM for each power plant individually before and after CCS to map regional variation in the costs and benefits of CCS. Running the ISRM for individual emissions sources may introduce error into the study as reduced-form air-quality models often run with a scaling assumption that errors due to simplifications of nonlinear atmospheric chemistry and physics are minimized when scaled across many sources and locations3,59,60. We therefore include additional results under different concentration–response functions for sensitivity in Supplementary Figs. 1 and 9.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

title: Indonesia's currency crisis: Fossil fuel dependence and subsidies a key driver
description:
The underappreciated driver of Indonesia’s currency crisis is fossil fuel dependence and subsidies, with budget deficit and a weakening trade balance playing a critical role and fossil fuels at the heart of the matter.
Fossil fuel dependence is a key driver of Indonesia’s crisis: the rise in the oil and gas import bill has decimated the country’s trade surplus, while fossil fuel price subsidies total around 13% of the state budget and 2% of the GDP.
Clean energy growth has lagged far behind growth in energy demand, with fossil fuels filling the gap.
Electrification, replacing the direct use of fossil fuels and biomass with electricity, is the key way to eliminate reliance on dirty fuels in transport, industry and households.
A thorough reckoning with the role of fossil fuels in the crisis will help calibrate the response.
text:
In early June, the value of the Indonesian rupiah fell to a record low against the US dollar, driving up imported food and fuel costs, accelerating inflation, forcing interest rate hikes and raising the cost of paying off foreign currency debt. The underappreciated driver of Indonesia’s currency crisis is fossil fuel dependence and subsidies, with budget deficit and a weakening trade balance playing a critical role and fossil fuels at the heart of the matter.

Fossil fuel dependence is a key driver of Indonesia’s crisis: the rise in the oil and gas import bill has decimated the country’s trade surplus, while fossil fuel price subsidies total around 13% of the state budget and 2% of the GDP.

Fossil fuel consumption subsidies, including budgeted losses to state-owned power and oil companies stemming from artificially low prices, will balloon to a projected USD 23bn this year, which is 10% of the national budget and a whopping 1.5% of the GDP.

Indonesia also cross-subsidizes domestic coal consumption to the tune of USD 6bn/year by forcing coal mining companies to sell at a discount to the national power company and other domestic consumers. If the same income transfer was made by taxing coal exports, it would boost government fiscal revenue by 4%.

Another key source of pressure on the currency is the weakening trade balance. The oil and gas import bill jumped 83% year-on-year in April while exports fell in value. As a result, the country’s usual trade surplus disappeared almost completely, plummeting to the weakest point since 2020.

Year-on-year changes in the value of Indonesia’s imports in April 2026, and an overview of foreign trade up to April, from Statistics Indonesia. (Migas=Oil&gas.)

The spike in oil prices hurts Indonesia because the net imports of oil and gas have already been rising steadily for years, reaching an all-time high in January 2026, just before the current crisis. This is driven by both the rise in consumption and decline in domestic production.

Net oil and gas imports in April and May also hit new records for the months after the Hormuz crisis was in full swing.

The share of clean, non-fossil power generation has barely increased in Indonesia over the past decade, and now lags well below the ASEAN average and other major Asian economies, a result of the state-owned utility being locked in to subsidized coal.

Unlike many other Asian economies, Indonesia also increased domestic gas consumption after the 2021-22 gas crisis, and has massive plans for gas-fired power plants over the next decade.

Clean energy growth has lagged far behind growth in energy demand, with fossil fuels filling the gap. There are hopeful signs however: the crisis seems to have given president Prabowo’s ambitious 100GW solar initiative the push it needed, and electrification is accelerating.

Electrification, replacing the direct use of fossil fuels and biomass with electricity, is the key way to eliminate reliance on dirty fuels in transport, industry and households. Indonesia has made progress on electrifying its energy use, but lags behind the leaders in Asia, including Vietnam, Malaysia and China.

Until recently, EV sales in Indonesia were far behind the Asian leaders, Vietnam and China, held back by subsidized fuel prices. This is changing as EV sales have been on a tear recently. It was too little too late to avert the current crisis but will help future-proof the country.

Recent responses by Indonesia’s leadership have been mixed, with a push to buy more Russian oil on the one hand and to advance the ambitious solar programme on the other.

A thorough reckoning with the role of fossil fuels in the crisis will help calibrate the response.

title: As Duke seeks higher rates, will gas plant plans collide with clean energy goals?

text:
Just a few years ago, North Carolina’s energy future looked very different.

For much of the last decade, utilities were planning for slow growth and a transition to cleaner energy. Today, soaring demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, manufacturing and population growth is forcing Duke Energy, regulators and lawmakers to rethink how North Carolina will generate enough electricity — and who will pay for it.

North Carolina law calls for carbon-neutral electricity generation by 2050. At the same time, Duke says meeting rapidly growing demand will require new natural gas plants. That has sparked debate over how the state can keep electricity reliable and affordable while still meeting its long-term climate goals. Environmental and consumer advocates have also questioned whether customers should bear the costs of new infrastructure built to serve data centers and other large power users.

“It’s hugely different than it was five to 10 years ago,” said Robert Cox, director of the Energy Production and Infrastructure Center at UNC Charlotte said of the rise in electricity demand. “Five years ago, nobody saw this coming.”

The debate sits at the center of Duke Energy’s latest long-range plan, the utility’s request for higher electric rates and a legislative push to reexamine parts of North Carolina’s clean-energy transition.

The utility is seeking roughly an 18% rate increase over three years for typical residential customers, arguing it needs major investments in generation, transmission and grid infrastructure to serve a rapidly growing region.

“Given the Carolinas’ exponential growth, we need all available economically viable resources – nuclear, renewables, storage, natural gas and coal – to meet the needs of our customers,” Duke Energy spokesperson Bill Norton said.”

One reason natural gas continues to play a major role is reliability. Unlike solar power, which depends on weather conditions, natural gas plants can ramp production up or down when demand changes.

“The future has changed. I think there is an economic driver that requires large power, and that’s why they’ve gone back to natural gas,” Cox said. “I mean it’s just the reality of where we’re at.”

How will Duke reach carbon neutrality while building new gas plants?

North Carolina law calls for carbon-neutral electricity generation by 2050. Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club, have questioned how long-lived natural gas facilities fit into that future and whether customers could ultimately be left paying for expensive modifications or technological upgrades.

But Duke argues the goals are compatible.

“We remain firmly on target for carbon neutrality by 2050,” Norton said.

The utility’s position is backed by a previous decision from state regulators.

In a November 2024 order, the North Carolina Utilities Commission concluded that a 35-year anticipated useful life for new natural gas generation was reasonable for planning purposes and determined the projects fit into North Carolina’s carbon plan.

The commission acknowledged uncertainty surrounding future technologies, particularly hydrogen, but concluded Duke identified ways the facilities could provide value in a carbon-neutral future. Carbon neutrality does not necessarily require eliminating all emissions. Utilities can also reach neutrality through a variety of strategies like carbon capture, sequestration and offsets.

Public Staff, the state agency responsible for representing utility customers before regulators, generally agreed a 35-year useful life assumption is reasonable. Dustin Metz, director of the Public Staff’s Energy Division, said equipment manufacturers and industry standards often place the expected useful life of natural gas assets at roughly 35 years.

However, Metz said long-term utility planning involves looking at a range of possible futures, including changes in fuel prices, regulations, construction costs and electricity demand.

For Cox, one of the biggest uncertainties may not be carbon capture or hydrogen. It may be forecasting demand itself.

Utilities across the country are preparing for massive growth tied to artificial intelligence and data centers, but questions remain about how many proposed projects will ultimately be built.

“One of the big risks ultimately may be that we begin to plan too much infrastructure relative to the number of data centers that actually get built,” Cox said.

NC house passes extensive data center bill

The debate over Duke’s plans has also reached the General Assembly.

On June 3, the North Carolina House approved Senate Bill 730, known as the Ratepayer Protection Act. In addition to imposing new guidelines and restrictions on data centers, the measure would require a study examining the current and projected effects of North Carolina’s carbon-neutrality requirements on residential, commercial and industrial electric bills.

The bill would also prohibit the Utilities Commission from approving the retirement of certain large coal and natural gas facilities until Duke Energy receives approval for a new nuclear project capable of generating at least 1,000 megawatts.

Supporters say the legislation would help protect ratepayers and ensure reliable electricity generation as demand grows. Critics argue it could slow the state’s transition away from fossil fuels.

Senate Bill 730 would tie certain retirement decisions to approval of a future nuclear project, but Duke’s own planning documents suggest the requirement may not significantly alter the utility’s current timeline.

Duke’s resource plan calls for seeking approval of a new nuclear project by the end of 2028, while its next major coal retirements are scheduled for 2029, meaning the legislation’s requirement could be satisfied before those retirements occur.

“Duke Energy is committed to its customers and communities and will continue working with policymakers and regulators to deliver reliable and increasingly clean energy while keeping rates as low as possible,” Norton said.
